Content:
Consider the standard basis [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}] of the Euclidean plane [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the unit square spanned by the vectors.

Content:
Let [MATH: [2|0; 0|1]] be a matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T.] We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: \mathbf{T}] as follows:
[MATH: i^{′}|= T(i) = [2|0; 0|1][1; 0] = [2; 0] = 2i; j^{′}|= T(j) = [2|0; 0|1][0; 1] = [0; 1] = j]

Content:
Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/913f713af57050bff01b5e79203d8e02]

Content:
We see that the transformation represented by the matrix [MATH: T] multiplies the vector [MATH: \mathbf{i}] by a factor of [MATH: 2] and leaves the vector [MATH: \mathbf j] unchanged. This type of transformation is called a stretch in the [MATH: \mathbf x]-direction. We can also call it a horizontal stretch. In this case, we have a horizontal stretch of scale factor [MATH: \mathbf 2.]

Content:
In general, a stretch in the [MATH: x]-direction of scale factor [MATH: k] with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix
[MATH: [k|0; 0|1]]

sections.normalized_html: A linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a stretch along the [MATH: x]-axis or [MATH: y]-axis. Given that [MATH: [− 4; 3]] and [MATH: [− 16; 3]] what is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}?]
sections.readable_text: A linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a stretch along the [MATH: x]-axis or [MATH: y]-axis. Given that [MATH: [− 4; 3]] and [MATH: [− 16; 3]] what is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we are told that [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a stretch along the [MATH: x]-axis or [MATH: y]-axis.

Comparing the [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-components of [MATH: \mathbf{v}] and [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}),] we note the following:

  • the [MATH: x]-component of [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})] is [MATH: 4] times the [MATH: x]-component of [MATH: \mathbf{v},] while

  • the [MATH: y]-components of [MATH: \mathbf{v}] and [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})] are the same.

So, we conclude that [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a stretch of scale factor [MATH: 4] in the [MATH: x]-direction.

Therefore, the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is [MATH: [4|0; 0|1]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the standard basis [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}] of the Euclidean plane [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the unit square spanned by the vectors.

Content:
Let [MATH: [2|0; 0|1]] be a matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T.] We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: \mathbf{T}] as follows:
[MATH: i^{′}|= T(i) = [2|0; 0|1][1; 0] = [2; 0] = 2i; j^{′}|= T(j) = [2|0; 0|1][0; 1] = [0; 1] = j]

Content:
Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/913f713af57050bff01b5e79203d8e02]

Content:
We see that the transformation represented by the matrix [MATH: T] multiplies the vector [MATH: \mathbf{i}] by a factor of [MATH: 2] and leaves the vector [MATH: \mathbf j] unchanged. This type of transformation is called a stretch in the [MATH: \mathbf x]-direction. We can also call it a horizontal stretch. In this case, we have a horizontal stretch of scale factor [MATH: \mathbf 2.]

Content:
In general, a stretch in the [MATH: x]-direction of scale factor [MATH: k] with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix
[MATH: [k|0; 0|1]]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Vertical Stretch

Content:
Now, let [MATH: [1|0; 0|2]] be a matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T.] We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: \mathbf T] as follows:
[MATH: i^{′}|= T(i) = [1|0; 0|2][1; 0] = [1; 0] = i; j^{′}|= T(j) = [1|0; 0|2][0; 1] = [0; 2] = 2j]

Content:
Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d4281f0df958135cfc892c1765a3df06]

Content:
The transformation represented by the matrix [MATH: T] multiplies the vector [MATH: \mathbf{j}] by [MATH: 2] and leaves the vector [MATH: \mathbf i] unchanged. This type of transformation is called a stretch in the [MATH: \mathbf y]-direction. We can also call this a vertical stretch. In this case, we have a vertical stretch of scale factor [MATH: \mathbf 2].

Content:
In general, a stretch in the [MATH: y]-direction of scale factor [MATH: k] with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix
[MATH: [1|0; 0|k]]

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding the Standard Matrix of a Stretch Transformation Given a Vector and its Image

Example Prompt:
A linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a stretch along the [MATH: x]-axis or [MATH: y]-axis. Given that [MATH: [− 4; 3]] and [MATH: [− 16; 3]] what is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we are told that [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a stretch along the [MATH: x]-axis or [MATH: y]-axis.

Comparing the [MATH: x]- and [MATH: y]-components of [MATH: \mathbf{v}] and [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}),] we note the following:

- the [MATH: x]-component of [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})] is [MATH: 4] times the [MATH: x]-component of [MATH: \mathbf{v},] while
- the [MATH: y]-components of [MATH: \mathbf{v}] and [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})] are the same.

So, we conclude that [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a stretch of scale factor [MATH: 4] in the [MATH: x]-direction.

Therefore, the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is
[MATH: [4|0; 0|1]]

Item 6 — Tutorial: Horizontal Shear

Content:
Consider the standard basis [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}] of the Euclidean plane [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the unit square spanned by the vectors.

Content:
Let [MATH: [1|0.5; 0|1]] be a matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T.] We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: \mathbf{T}] as follows:
[MATH: i^{′}|= T(i) = [1|0.5; 0|1][1; 0] = [1; 0] = i; j^{′}|= T(j) = [1|0.5; 0|1][0; 1] = [0.5; 1] = 0.5i + j]

Content:
Applying this transformation, we obtain the following image:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/12b52dfba1b01fdd1f6a270330eef8d8]

Content:
The transformation represented by the matrix [MATH: T] adds [MATH: 0.5\mathbf{i}] to [MATH: \mathbf j,] while the vector [MATH: \mathbf i] remains unchanged. This type of transformation is called a horizontal shear. In this case, we have a horizontal shear with a shear factor of [MATH: \mathbf{0.5}.]

Content:
In general, a horizontal shear of scale factor [MATH: k] with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix
[MATH: [1|k; 0|1]]

Item 7 — Tutorial: Vertical Shear

Content:
Now, let [MATH: [1|0; 0.5|1]] be a matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T.] We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: \mathbf{T}] as follows:
[MATH: i^{′}|= T(i) = [1|0; 0.5|1][1; 0] = [1; 0.5] = i + 0.5j; j^{′}|= T(j) = [1|0; 0.5|1][0; 1] = [0; 1] = j]

The transformation represented by the matrix [MATH: T] adds [MATH: 0.5\mathbf{j}] to [MATH: \mathbf i,] while the vector [MATH: \mathbf j] remains unchanged. This type of transformation is called a vertical shear. In this case, we have a vertical shear with a shear factor of [MATH: \mathbf{0.5}.]

Content:
In general, a vertical shear of scale factor [MATH: k] with its center at the origin is represented by the matrix
